newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria cabinet backs opening secret police files.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria cabinet backs opening secret police files.

text.p: Bulgaria's cabinet approved a draft bill on Monday allowing communist-era police files to be opened to prevent any attempts to blackmail politicians, Deputy Prime Minister Vesselin Metodiev said.

"Today the government approved a draft bill aimed at opening secret files of the former State Security Service in a bid to avoid further speculation and blackmail among politicians," Metodiev told reporters.
Under the draft law, the files of members of parliament, ministers, senior government officials and high-ranking judges will be opened.
The draft will now be submitted to parliament, which is dominated by the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), which pledged to open the files in its manifesto for April elections.
"This bill is an attempt and expression of our will to revise our view of our recent history," Metodiev said.
To protect national security, the names of agents still working for the security service will be kept secret.

The State Security Service was dissolved in 1989 and its files are kept by the interior and defence ministries, the National Intelligence Service and the National Protection Service, which assures security for public figures.
The agencies would be required to submit the relevant files to the prime minister a month after the law was passed. All information will be made public in parliament, Metodiev said.
People who were spied on by the State Security will have access to their personal files but will not be allowed to give information about other people mentioned in them.
One year after the law is enforced, the files will be transferred to the National Archive and made available to the general public, Metodiev said.

Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev said in April he felt it was now too late to open the files because he believed they have been subject to tampering. More than seven years since the end of one-party rule have given ample opportunity for records to be forged, substituted or destroyed.
Bulgaria's communist secret service, closely allied to the Soviet KGB, had a network of 100,000 agents and informers.

Opening secret police files has been a controversial step even in former East Germany, although made easier by the clean break the former communist state made with the past by unifying with West Germany and disbanding its own intelligence service.
Debate on what to do with the files has taken up a large amount of parliamentary time in the past seven years but the issue has never been resolved.
Several prominent UDF figures, including former leaders Filip Dimitrov and Petar Beron, have been accused of having cooperated with the security services.

A former intelligence officer said last week that Ahmed Dogan, leader of the ethnic Turks' Movement for Rights and Freedoms and chairman of a coalition which forms the third biggest bloc in parliament, had been recruited when he was a student.
